overview: This file brings together cross-reference sheets and diplomatic correspondence concerning the official designation, international legal status, and sovereignty of the Kwantung Leased Territory—especially Dairen—from 1930 to 1937. It documents Japan’s position on the 1907 Dairen customs agreement following recognition of Manchukuo, competing interpretations of the expiry or extension of Japan’s lease, and later requests from the U.S. Treasury Department and a New York firm for an authoritative statement of Dairen’s status. The concluding State Department reply traces the territory’s transfer from China to Russia and then Japan while emphasizing that the original lease did not extinguish Chinese sovereignty.

people.name: Maxwell M. Hamilton
people.role: Chief, Division of Far Eastern Affairs, U.S. Department of State

people.name: John Van Antwerp MacMurray
people.role: Author and compiler of the cited collection of treaties and agreements concerning China

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to despatch on the official designation of Kwantung
subfiles.about: The sheet points to despatch no. 93 concerning the official English designation of the government of the Kwantung Leased Territory.
subfiles.summary: This filing note refers researchers to despatch no. 93 in file 800.114 N 16, Information/228. The referenced despatch, sent from Japan by Castle, addressed the official English name of the territorial government administering the Kwantung Leased Territory.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to Johnson telegram on Dairen and Manchukuo
subfiles.about: The sheet points to telegram no. 1126 concerning Japan’s legal argument about the Dairen customs agreement, Manchukuo, and the Liaodong lease.
subfiles.summary: This note cross-references telegram no. 1126 in file 693.002 Manchuria/268. Its précis states that Japan preferred negotiated abrogation of the Dairen agreement but argued that Nanking’s rejection of the 1915 treaty logically entailed expiration of Japan’s Liaodong lease in 1923.

subfiles.title: Johnson telegram reporting Japan’s position on Dairen customs
subfiles.about: Johnson transmits a Reuters report explaining Japan’s position on the Dairen customs agreement and the possible transfer of leased territory to Manchukuo.
subfiles.summary: The telegram relays a Reuters report from Tokyo stating that Japan would not approach China to negotiate abrogation of the 1907 Dairen customs agreement. If China protested Manchukuo’s takeover of the Dairen customs service, Japan would argue that recognition of Manchukuo had already rendered the agreement void. A Foreign Office spokesman also linked Nanking’s rejection of the 1915 treaty to the supposed 1923 expiration of the Liaodong lease and suggested that Japan might return the territory to Manchukuo if extraterritoriality were abolished, thereby strengthening the new state’s position and prestige.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to Treasury inquiry about the country containing Dairen
subfiles.about: The sheet points to a Treasury letter requesting the official name of the country in which Dairen, within the Kwantung Leased Territory, should be placed.
subfiles.summary: This filing note refers to a Treasury Department letter in file 142.14/1577. The letter concerned the port of Dairen and requested advice on the official country designation applicable to the port within the Kwantung Leased Territory.

subfiles.title: Treasury referral of the Barnes, Richardson & Colburn inquiry
subfiles.from: Wayne C. Taylor, Assistant Secretary of the Treasury
subfiles.about: The Treasury Department forwards a private firm’s inquiry concerning Dairen’s political status in 1935 to the State Department.
subfiles.summary: Taylor encloses a copy of the November 8 letter from Barnes, Richardson & Colburn asking about Dairen’s political status in 1935. He explains that the firm has been told its inquiry was referred to the Secretary of State for reply. The associated papers were received by the State Department’s Historical Adviser on November 13.

subfiles.title: Treasury acknowledgment to Barnes, Richardson & Colburn
subfiles.about: The Treasury Department acknowledges the firm’s inquiry and advises that it has been referred to the Department of State.
subfiles.summary: The letter acknowledges receipt of the firm’s November 8 request for information about the political status of “Darien, China” in 1935. Because the matter falls more properly within State Department jurisdiction, the Treasury has sent a copy of the inquiry to the Secretary of State for a response.

subfiles.title: Barnes, Richardson & Colburn inquiry on Dairen sovereignty
subfiles.about: A New York firm asks whether the United States regarded Dairen in 1935 as Chinese sovereign territory or as Japanese territory by virtue of a leasehold.
subfiles.summary: Barnes, Richardson & Colburn asks the Treasury Department to define the 1935 political status of “Darien, China.” The firm specifically seeks to know whether the United States considered the city to be under Chinese sovereignty or Japanese sovereignty because of Japan’s leasehold interest.

subfiles.title: State Department reply on the legal status of Dairen
subfiles.from: Maxwell M. Hamilton, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: The State Department explains Dairen’s legal position by tracing the Kwantung lease from China to Russia and then Japan.
subfiles.summary: Hamilton explains that Dairen lies within the approximately 1,300-square-mile Kwantung Leased Territory, which China leased to Russia in 1898 for twenty-five years while expressly retaining sovereignty. Under the 1905 Treaty of Portsmouth, Russia transferred the lease of Port Arthur, Dairen, adjacent territory, and territorial waters to Japan with China’s consent, and China confirmed the transfer later that year. A 1915 agreement extended the leases of Port Arthur and Dalny, along with the terms of the South Manchuria and Antung–Mukden railways, to ninety-nine years. The reply cites MacMurray’s treaty collection as the source for the relevant texts.

interest: The file is valuable because it juxtaposes day-to-day filing practice with substantive American diplomatic reasoning about sovereignty, leases, recognition, customs administration, and extraterritoriality. The 1932 telegram captures Japan’s effort to use recognition of Manchukuo and China’s rejection of the 1915 agreement to justify unilateral changes at Dairen, while the 1937 State Department letter offers a compact legal genealogy of the territory without conceding that the lease extinguished Chinese sovereignty. The papers also preserve shifting and erroneous Western forms of regional place-names—Dairen, Darien, Dalny, Liatong, and Liaotung—which are useful for tracing contemporary terminology and archival indexing.
